issue_context.title: Warn when a dynamically imported chunk is statically imported
issue_context.body:
### Description

When I dynamically import a file/chunk from a file, I want the bundler to make sure that chunk remains dynamically loaded in the future. For example, when another file accidentally loads the file/chunk statically.

_index.js_
```js
import './file-a.js';
import './file-b.js';
```

_file-a.js_
```js
import('./chunk');
```

_file-b.js_
```js
import './chunk'; // This should be flagged
```




### Suggested solution

Dev/build warning:
```
"./chunk.js" is dynamically imported from "./file-a.js", but "./file-b.js" imports it statically so it cannot be chunked.
```


### Alternative

_No response_

### Additional context

In one of my projects, a dynamic import was utilized to code-split & defer loading a large file. However, later on from a different part of the project, I mistakenly imported the file statically which negated the optimization by removing the code-split. I didn't notice this for a while and was affecting the load time of the app.

If this can happen to a single-person codebase, I think it's very likely to happen to a larger code-base. I think Vite is perfectly positioned to catch simple mistakes like this.

### Validations

- [X] Follow our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)
- [X] Read the [Contributing Guidelines](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [X] Read the [docs](https://vitejs.dev/guide).
- [X] Check that there isn't already an issue that request the same feature to avoid creating a duplicate.
comments:
I don't think we are able to provide such a feature during bundling due to many limitations:

- One js module is not necessarily corresponded to one output chunk. It may be bundled with other modules or splitted into multiple chunks.
- If module dynamically imported imports its parent it will not be splitted into a separeted chunk. The proposed feature will not detect such a situation.
- How to deal with virtual modules?
- For a specific module it may be imported dynamically or statically many times from its entry, which creates a race condition we cannot determine. This feature only works between all statically imported module to the others.

So I think this feature may not be pratical to implement.

Implementation should be straightforward: check every chunk to see if contains a dynamic import to another module in the same chunk. I believe Rollup already provides a graph of chunks, the modules they contain, and how they're requested.

Virtual modules doesn't matter here, but how they're loaded does (static vs dynamic import).

Let me clarify a bit more:

* Giving out such a warning as the issue shown may be difficult, since the js module may be splitted into multiple chunks.
* We can calculate the import graph of chunks during dev/build. The detection algorithm checks if each entry has two different import path to any other individual chunk, where one of the path is purely static and the other one contains dynamic import edge.
* The detection algorithm won't work if the graph contains loops, i.e. there are circular dependencies.
* The detection algorithm cannot detect from any chunk other than the entry. If the detection starts from middle chunk, the middle chunk may be dynamically imported by other chunk, which creates a race condition that the detection algo won't be useful.
* Finally, while the intention of such a warning is to prevent accidentally statically import some large chunk you want to dynamically import, the pattern "Imported a chunk both statically and dynamically" here is not necessarily an anti-pattern:

For example, I wrote a small nice format util function:

```js
function myLittleFormat(s) {
  return `Formatted:${s}`
}
```

And I intentionally use this format function everywhere in my code base -- both static-loaded chunks and dynamic-loaded chunks. The function will be splitted into a single chunk and be imported statically and dynamically, which matches the pattern and produce a warning. Is this really matters that such a chunk get imported both statically and dynamically to give a warning?

Or we have some components like `<MyButton />` that needs to be loaded in the first screen and used in some dynamically imported pages. This will also match the pattern, Should we give a warning here?

It is hard to calculate or draw a red line of how large a chunk and its imports are as well as detect the pattern every time an import edge is added to the import graph, which may lead to performance drop during dev/build. I concluded it is not worth adding such a feature.

At this stage, I think discussion will be more fruitful if we dive deeper into the root problem and discuss alternative solutions rather than speculating implementation challenges. Do you have an alternative proposal?

----

I do think there are some misunderstandings though, so I created a quick demo:
https://stackblitz.com/edit/node-nlhpad?file=index.mjs,src%2Ffile-b.js

Essentially, when a file is imported with mixed imports, it's likely a mistake and a warning should be emitted.

The repo and the algorithm you showed are just the same as what I had said. The root problems here are:

* You think the pattern "Imported a chunk both statically and dynamically" should give some warnings.
* You think we can create an algorithm to detect such pattern.

However:

* The pattern described above is not necessarily an anti-pattern and such warnings are considered false alarms.
* Such an algorithm has many limitations and may face performance drops. 

I don't think we should ever try to detect such a pattern and thus offer no alternatives, sorry for that.

This is the root problem I'm trying to address (from the issue):

> In one of my projects, a dynamic import was utilized to code-split & defer loading a large file. However, later on from a different part of the project, I mistakenly imported the file statically which negated the optimization by removing the code-split. I didn't notice this for a while and was affecting the load time of the app.
>
> If this can happen to a single-person codebase, I think it's very likely to happen to a larger code-base. I think Vite is perfectly positioned to catch simple mistakes like this.

I don't think this is an anti-pattern either, but typically when people opt-into code-splitting, they don't mean to opt-out of it too. Anyway, I'd love to hear more about your points. Have you investigated this in anyway? Would you be able to demonstrate your points with code like I did?

Also, just to clarify, you're not a [Vite team member](https://vitejs.dev/team.html), correct?

In your index.js, change the context into

```js
import('./file-a.js');
import('./file-b.js');
```

Your algorithm won't flag it with a warning. But it is possible when people may accidentally do the import mistake as stated in your issue in async modules such as page chunk of spa.

I give the content/scenarios of the staticly-and-dynamicly-imported module to demonstrate that it may not be appropriate to throw a warning.

No I am not a vite core member. They are labeled with "member" so you actually don't need to ask. I may not be right here but I think this is all I want to say. Feel free to continue if you have made any progress further on this issue.
Your code seems to be failed to detect `chunk.js` which get both statically imported and dynamically imported: https://stackblitz.com/edit/node-sfkvpx?file=index.mjs

When I speculated there was a misunderstanding earlier, it was based on this:
> Or we have some components like `<MyButton />` that needs to be loaded in the first screen and used in some dynamically imported pages. This will also match the pattern, Should we give a warning here?

Based on your reproduction, I think there definitely is a misunderstanding.

The algorithm is working expectedly because in the two chunks your repro generates, there are no async imports _within_ them. I'm only trying to detect mixed imports to a module _within_ a chunk  (e.g. this can only happen if both `import './file.js'` and `import('./file.js')` exists within the same chunk). If the a parent module is dynamically imported like your repro shows, so statically imported modules are duplicated across chunks, that's a different problem and it's not relevant to the issue I'm addressing. 

Anyway, I'm not sure if this discussion is productive and I think it's making it difficult for others to engage. I'm considering starting a new thread.

Sorry for the misunderstanding. A warning will be presented when a chunk is both dynamically and statically importing the exact same chunk then. No children will be tracked. This narrows down the detection and make it possible, and I cannot put more code on the dynamic side. However, I can put more code on the static side to trigger this warning: https://stackblitz.com/edit/node-kh6xxm?file=src%2Ffile-a.js,src%2Ffile-b.js,src%2Fcomponent-alt.js,src%2Fcomponent.js

It seems this issue is driven far from your proposal due to my misunderstanding. Sorry for screwing it up. Feel free to open a new thread.

This sounds like a nice feature to support builtin. I'm not sure if it's easy to support in dev because we currently don't keep the information of whether is module is dynamically or statically imported in the module graph. In build, rollup provides this with `ModuleInfo.importers` and `ModuleInfo.dynamicImporters`.

I guess this could start of as an external Vite plugin if you're interested, and maybe we can support build-time only for now.

review_comments:
Nice catch! That will be a false positive warning. I think we have 4 circumstances for this case.

1.  both importers and dynamic importers in the same chunk with module
    ⚠️ should warn, dynamic imports do not make the module into another chunk.
2.  only importers in the same chunk with the module
   🟢 should not warn, dynamic importers don't share a chunk with the module.
3. only dynamic importers in the chunk with module
   ⚠️ should warn, should not be in the same chunk.
4. importers and dynamic importers are both not in the chunk with the module
   🟢 should not warn.

So IIUC, if we add this judging condition: **when dynamic importer shares a chunk with the module**, will be enough for this case. Also, find a false positive warning previously.

I'm horrible with following things up, but I'm here again 😄 

That's an interesting deduction, admittedly it took me quite a while to figure out why, but I think I'm slowly getting it. It would be nice to document a part of this behaviour in-code too.

With that I think we can test this out in the next minor beta. Thanks for improving this!
Following up is greatly appreciated 🙌! I added a concise comment in the code. Do you think it's enough for others to understand?

To be honest I don't quite understand the comment well 😅 It does explain what it's doing, but I'm not sure why it's doing it that way. The PR link is a nice touch for those who want to follow in the future though.

Here's some questions I have while reading the code:
1. If the chunk's modules have both `importers` and `dynamicImporters`, why is that bad? (I think the initial comment explains this well but it could be elaborated.)
2. Re:

    ```js
          for (const dynamicImporter of module.dynamicImporters) {
             if (chunk.moduleIds.includes(dynamicImporter)) {
    ```
    Why do we check the `dynamicImporters` and not `importers`?
3. And, why do we check if the `dynamicImporter` (of the current chunk module) is part of `chunk.moduleIds`? What does this relation mean? Or, what makes this chunk/module special?

But also, if you've copied https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/12850#discussion_r1196949015 into the code I wouldn't mind too 😅 Just that I also had trouble trying to understand that one. It could also be just me.

Let me try to explain it clearly, feel free to correct me if there's anything is wrong.
1. To address the original issue, we need to find a module both static imported and dynamic imported. If so, the deliberate dynamic import does not work as expected.
2. and 3. IIUC,  `chunk.modulesIds` contains the modules in this chunk and `module.dynamicImporters` and `module.importers` is a set of all modules of importers and dynamic importers that are **not** only in the current chunk. So we need to filter out the intersection of dynamic importers and sibling modules in the same chunk. The intersection, as described above, is not expected to work (A dynamically imports B, but they are in the same chunk). Then we warn it out.

Hope I made it clear this time 😜

Ah thanks I think I get it now! So a chunk's modules (`moduleIds`) have `importers` and `dynamicImporters`. And both importers could be combined into the same current chunk by Rollup. However, when a dynamic importer is found in the same chunk, that means there really isn't a dynamic import happening, hence we will warn. A normal importer found in the same chunk is fine because that's not what we're concerned of.

I think we can put your comment above as the in-code comment 👍 

I was also confused as I thought we need to crawl the module graph to get it completely correct. E.g in this [stackblitz example](https://stackblitz.com/edit/stackblitz-starters-xl6qsw?description=Starter%20project%20for%20Node.js,%20a%20JavaScript%20runtime%20built%20on%20Chrome%27s%20V8%20JavaScript%20engine&file=src%2Fmain.js,index.mjs&title=node.new%20Starter) (note: the latest Rollup version has a different chunk output than the link I gave above before), it doesn't correctly warn for `chunk.js` being imported by `main.js` and transitively dynamically imported by `main.js` through `foo.js` too. Traversing the `dynamicImporters` of the `module.importers` should fix this I think. But I don't think this is a huge deal for now and we can improve it later.

Ah, I realized that we're only detecting direct cases here. The indirect cases are ignored.
However, in the example above, I think the result is correct for me 🤔. `main.js` statically imports `chunk.js` so it's expected they're in the same chunk. `foo.js` is in a different chunk from `main.js` which is also good for me.
Anyway, we could try to add this into the codebase first to see how users feel in real projects. Crawling the graph could cover all cases, but might warn some cases while the code should be like that, I guess.

Hmm yeah I guess it's a bit detable whether the stackblitz example is an issue, since technically for `import('./foo')` the intent _is_ that `foo` becomes a separate chunk and it is one eventually. Let's move forward with this for now then.
